title: Feedback That Changes Behaviour
performance: The viewer takes a vague comment they were about to give a colleague and rewrites it so it names one specific observed behaviour, the real effect it had, and one concrete next step, before they say it.

audience.assumed_prior: Knows feedback matters; usually delivers general praise or criticism; has received vague feedback themselves.
audience.why: They give feedback to peers or direct reports and want a colleague to actually do something differently.
audience.motivation: Get a colleague to change a habit without damaging the relationship.
audience.context: Short corporate video, likely watched at a desk between meetings; expertise reversal applies, so one short worked example and decisions sooner.

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: The skill is rewriting one comment. One running example (Sam, the meeting habit, one comment) lets the viewer watch the comment change part by part, then try a faded version in the check and an independent one afterwards. Practitioners need a short worked example, not a lecture.
strategy.signature_move: Show the vague comment, add behaviour, add effect, add one next step, reread the whole comment, then let the viewer rewrite a new one.

misconceptions.belief: Warm, general praise is enough to keep or change what someone does.
misconceptions.why_tempting: It feels kind, the receiver smiles, and the relationship stays comfortable. Praise can still support the relationship, but alone it rarely guides behaviour (F3).

misconceptions.belief: Naming the person's character or motive ('you're dominating', 'you don't care') is clearer and more honest than describing what happened.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Labels feel like the real point of the problem and are quick to say. But a label is a judgement, and character-aimed feedback is more likely to trigger defensiveness (F5, F6, F8).

misconceptions.belief: A thorough list of changes is more helpful than one small step.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Covering everything feels diligent and fair to the receiver. One small next step is easier to act on than a long list (F10).

hook.sketch: Imagine a manager says after a meeting, 'Great energy in there today,' and Sam, who often cuts colleagues off, beams and nods. Next week Sam does exactly the same thing. On-screen essence: 'Sam felt great. Nothing changed.'

arc.promise: Stay with Sam and that meeting, and you will leave able to turn a comment like that into feedback a colleague can act on.
arc.bridge_from_prior: You have been Sam: someone said something nice and vague, you felt fine, and nothing about what you did changed. Good intentions were never the problem; the comment gave nothing to hold on to.

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a warm, vague comment tends to leave what someone does unchanged
concepts: Vague feedback tends to give nothing specific to repeat or change (F2)
Warm praise can feel good without saying which action to keep (F3)
sections.recap_after: One line: a feeling moved, behaviour did not.

sections.goal: the viewer can rewrite a vague comment so it names a specific observed behaviour
concepts: A behaviour is something that could be seen or heard; a label is a judgement (F5)
Anchor in what the person said or did in a particular situation (F4)
Character-aimed feedback is more likely to trigger defensiveness (F6)
sections.recap_after: The comment now says what Sam did: spoke over Priya while she was mid-point.

sections.goal: the viewer can use an observed effect and one concrete next step to complete the rewritten comment
concepts: State the effect as what actually happened, such as a point left unfinished or a decision delayed, not a guess at motives (F7, F8)
End with one small concrete next step, ideally agreed with the person (F9, F10, F12)
Behaviour, effect and next step is one useful structure; others exist (F13)
sections.recap_after: Reread the whole comment: behaviour, effect, one step, in plain words. What CHANGES on screen: the single comment gains a part at a time, and the earlier version fades behind it.

sections.goal: the viewer can distinguish the rewrite that names behaviour, effect and next step from rewrites that miss one
concepts: Three-question test: observable, real effect, one step the person could try (F14)
New small moment: a colleague who starts a call without the agenda
sections.recap_after: The test is three questions, and the answer card shows which part each wrong option missed.

sections.goal: the viewer can use the same three parts to rewrite a real comment they owe this week
concepts: Pick one real piece of feedback owed this week and rewrite it before saying it
Return to Sam: reworked comment, next week the habit shifts (payoff)
sections.recap_after: Sam's next-week meeting: he lets Priya finish. What CHANGES on screen: the same meeting scene, before and after.

arc.payoff: Back to Sam and the meeting: the same moment, now with the reworked comment (behaviour, effect, one step). Next week Sam lets Priya finish her point first. It answers the hook: this time something concrete had changed, not just a feeling. Specific feedback makes change easier, it does not guarantee it.

practice_ladder.description: Sam's comment rewritten step by step on screen.
A new small moment; the viewer picks the rewrite that has all three parts.
The viewer rewrites a real comment they owe this week.

recall_moments.prompt: Sam's comment now says what he did. What does it still not say?

recall_moments.question: Priya starts a call without the agenda and the decision slips to next week. Which comment would you give?
options: A: 'Thanks for your effort today, but you need to be more organised.'
B: 'You started the call without the agenda, so the decision slipped to next week. Could you send it round the day before next time?'
C: 'You started without the agenda and the decision slipped to next week. Please be more prepared.'
recall_moments.answer: B names what happened, the real effect, and one step the person could try.
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: C: it names behaviour and effect, so it feels complete, but 'be more prepared' is not a concrete step. A is the other miss: a label with no behaviour, effect or step.

transfer_tasks.task: Pick one piece of feedback you owe a colleague this week. Write it as: what they did, what it led to, one thing to try. Check it with the three questions (observable? real effect? one step?) before you say it.
transfer_tasks.context: Own job, own colleague, within the week.

gagne.guidance: strategy.signature_move and the worked example in s2 and s3
gagne.practice: recall_moments quiz after s3 and practice_ladder faded and independent rungs; s5 task

merrill.problem_centred: One running problem: Sam and the meeting comment, in every section
merrill.demonstration: s2 and s3 show the comment changing part by part
merrill.integration: s5 and transfer_tasks[0]: a real comment owed this week

mayer.coherence: one example, one loud thing at a time, no decoration
mayer.signalling: the changed part of the comment is highlighted at each step
mayer.redundancy: on-screen text is the comment itself, narration adds the why, not a repeat
mayer.contiguity: each new part appears beside the narration that names it
mayer.segmenting: one part of the comment per step in s2 and s3
mayer.pre_training: s1 names the problem before the parts are taught

arcs.attention: hook: a nice comment and no change
arcs.relevance: the viewer's own colleague and feedback owed this week
arcs.confidence: short worked example, then a three-question test
arcs.satisfaction: the payoff shows the habit shifting next week

flags: DURATION-NOTE: 120 s was requested and used. At this length no section can be a rest over 180 s; s1 is the rest valley, kept short. Gate rule on rest over 180 s cannot be met honestly in a 2-minute video.
HOOK-NEEDS-FACT: the Sam scene is invented, framed as 'imagine'; the knowledge sheet gives no real case.

Not verified: the knowledge sheet was not checked against external sources (its own review note). Say 'tends to' and 'more likely to', never 'always'. Optional facts F11 (timing) and F12 (ask for their view) are mentioned only lightly because of the 2-minute length.

Open question carried from brief: the organisation's own feedback model is unknown; the plan presents behaviour, effect and next step as one useful structure, not the only one (F13). Classic story-cartoon treatment assumed; newer treatments can be offered later.
